chief_complaint: core body temperature 41.2C, profound delirium/coma, and hot dry skin in marathon runner collapsing across finish line on hot humid day
hpi_details: 34M runner presenting with core temp 41.2C, encephalopathy, and rhabdomyolysis requiring immediate rapid evaporative cooling (ice water immersion or cold mist fan spraying) target core temp <38.9C along with aggressive IV crystalloid hydration.
ideas: His running partner thinks he pushed himself far past his limit in the sweltering heat without drinking enough water.
concerns: His partner is terrified that his dangerously high body temperature is causing irreversible damage to his brain or organs.
expectations: His partner hopes the emergency team can quickly cool him down with ice baths and give him IV fluids to wake him up.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Heat Stroke (exertional) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Heat Stroke Exertional Hyperthermia, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Heat Stroke (exertional).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Heat exhaustion (less severe, normal mental status) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Altered mental status with very high temperature — this combination defines heat stroke and demands immediate cooling.

Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Heat Stroke Exertional Hyperthermia: core body temperature 41.2C, profound delirium/coma, and hot dry skin in marathon runner collapsing across finish line on hot humid day. 34M runner presenting with core temp 41.2C, encephalopathy, and rhabdomyolysis requiring immediate rapid evaporative cooling (ice water immersion or cold mist fan spraying) target core temp <38.9C along with aggressive IV crystalloid hydration.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Heat Stroke Exertional Hyperthermia.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Heat Stroke Exertional Hyperthermia.
reference_soap.plan: Begin immediate rapid cooling, preferably cold-water immersion for exertional heat stroke, without delaying for tests; monitor core temperature continuously and stop cooling at about 38.9°C. Support airway and circulation, give IV crystalloid guided by perfusion and urine output, and monitor/treat rhabdomyolysis, electrolyte abnormalities, renal injury, liver injury, and coagulopathy. Antipyretics do not treat heat stroke. Admit for critical-care level monitoring.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Heat Stroke Exertional Hyperthermia

Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Extreme exertion in heat overwhelms the body's cooling mechanisms, causing core temperature above 40°C with altered mental status — a true emergency needing rapid cooling (ice water immersion) as the single most important intervention.
differentials: Heat exhaustion (less severe, normal mental status)
red_flags: Altered mental status with very high temperature — this combination defines heat stroke and demands immediate cooling

must_ask.say: What were you doing, and how hot and humid was it?
How alert is he — is he confused or unresponsive?
How much fluid was he drinking during the race?
Is his skin hot and dry, or still sweating?
When did he collapse, and how long has he been like this?

history.answer: I collapsed right after crossing the marathon finish line, and I feel burning hot all over and completely out of it.
It started suddenly right at the end of the race about thirty minutes ago, and my body has been burning hot since.
The medics said my temperature spiked over 41 degrees, and it has stayed blazing hot without any chills or shivering.
No, I haven't taken any acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or other fever medicines today.
I don't have any cough, phlegm, or sore throat, but my breathing feels very fast and shallow.
I haven't had any burning when I urinate or flank pain, but I haven't passed any urine since early this morning.
I threw up once right after I fell at the finish line, but I don't have any stomach cramps or diarrhea.
My head is throbbing horribly, and I felt completely confused and blacked out for a few minutes after collapsing.
No, I don't have any rash, insect bite marks, black scabs, or pain in my joints.
No, I haven't had any night sweats or lost any weight before today.
No, I haven't felt any swollen or painful lumps in my neck, armpits, or groin.
I haven't traveled overseas or had any contact with animals, just running the city marathon this morning.
No one around me is sick with a fever, cold, or any contagious illness.
No, I have never had cancer, chemotherapy, or taken any steroids or immune suppressants.
No, I have never had heart valve problems, and I haven't had any dental work done recently.
No, I haven't started any new prescription drugs or supplements in the past few months.
I have been with my wife for ten years with no other partners, and I have never used illegal or injected drugs.
I was running a full 42-kilometer marathon in blazing sun, and it was over 32 degrees Celsius and very humid.
I only took small sips of water at a couple of stations because my stomach felt full, so I barely drank anything.
My skin feels like an oven and totally dry; I noticed I stopped sweating during the last few miles.
My vision blurred and my legs gave out completely the second I crossed the finish line.
I don't remember much right after falling, and the race volunteers said I was talking nonsensically.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol two years ago.
I had my appendix removed when I was sixteen, but I haven't had any other surgeries or hospital stays.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure.
I have no allergies to any medications, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional beer on weekends, and I haven't had any alcohol for the past two weeks.
I work as an office accountant and live at home with my wife.
My father has high blood pressure, but there's no family history of anesthesia reactions, heart problems, or early deaths.
We were finishing the race together and I think he just completely overheated and collapsed from pushing too hard in this humidity.
I'm terrified that his body is literally cooking from the inside and that he might end up with permanent brain damage.
I'm hoping you can get his temperature down right away with ice packs and fluids so he safely wakes up.

exam.finding: Flushed, acutely ill male lying on gurney, visibly confused and breathing rapidly.
Severe hyperthermia at 41.2°C, sinus tachycardia, hypotension, and tachypnea.
Confused and disoriented to time and place; follows simple one-step commands with delayed response.
Skin is markedly hot, dry, and flushed with no active sweating, rash, petechiae, or insect eschars.
Neck is supple with full range of motion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Oral mucosa is dry with dry lips; posterior pharynx is clear without erythema or exudate.
Both tympanic membranes are clear with normal light reflex and no erythema.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or submandibular lymphadenopathy.
Tachycardic regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Soft, non-tender throughout without rebound tenderness or hepatosplenomegaly.
